claim: SIMON-128 implemented on Xilinx Artix-7 (xc7a35tcsg324-1) uses only 45 LUTs (0.22% of 20,800 available), 12 LUTRAM, and 27 FFs (0.06% of 4,600).
stance_target: extremely lightweight FPGA cipher cores are feasible undergraduate projects with tiny resource footprint

claim: The SIMON-128 Artix-7 implementation consumes only 0.072 W total on-chip power, a 69.87% reduction vs Zynq-7000 (239 mW) and 70.56% reduction vs Virtex-7 (248 mW).
stance_target: low-cost Artix-7 platform gives strong power efficiency for lightweight crypto cores versus larger FPGA families
scope_conditions: comparison against SIMON on Zynq-7000 and Virtex-7 from cited prior work [21]
quoted_support: We note a gain in power consumption of 69.87% compared to Zynq-7000 and 70.56% compared to Virtex-7, a gain in delay of 26.69% compared to Zynq-7000 and 8.95% compared to Virtex-7.

claim: The Artix-7 SIMON-128 implementation achieves a delay of 4.020 ns, an improvement of 26.69% over Zynq-7000 (5.448 ns) and 8.95% over Virtex-7 (4.415 ns).
stance_target: performance/delay superiority claim of Artix-7 low-cost platform for lightweight ciphers
scope_conditions: Table V comparison, same cipher across three FPGA families

claim: SIMON-128 is a Feistel-network symmetric block cipher designed by NSA researchers, prioritizing minimal hardware footprint for constrained embedded systems.
stance_target: background on SIMON algorithm as a project topic
quoted_support: One of SIMON's security goals was to keep a reasonable level of security in an environment where power, memory and processors are severely limited.
